stimulus.text: Men being, as has been said, by nature, all free, equal, and independent, no one can be put out of this estate, and subjected to the political power of another, without his own consent. The great and chief end, therefore, of men's uniting into commonwealths, and putting themselves under government, is the preservation of their property. Whenever the legislators endeavour to take away and destroy the property of the people, or to reduce them to slavery under arbitrary power, they put themselves into a state of war with the people, who are thereupon absolved from any farther obedience.
stimulus.source_note: John Locke, Second Treatise of Government (1689), abridged. Public domain.

books.section: A. Protestant Evangelicalism and Enlightenment Philosophy

primary_sources: John Locke, Second Treatise of Government (1689)

stem: In this passage, Locke says the chief end of government is the preservation of the people's “property.” What does Locke mean by property here?

options.text: Life, liberty, and estate — the broad goods of a person's life
Land and houses owned by wealthy planters and merchants
options.misconception: Locke's property is far broader than real estate — it covers life and liberty too.

options.text: Tax revenue collected by the government for public works
options.misconception: Revenue is what government collects, not what Locke says government exists to preserve.

options.text: The colonies' trade goods shipped to Britain under the Navigation Acts
options.misconception: Trade goods are one kind of estate, but Locke's property means much more than cargo.

rationales.A: For Locke, property means life, liberty, and estate together — everything a person has a right to keep. Government exists to preserve that whole bundle, not one item in it.
rationales.B: Land is only one part of Locke's property. His chief end covers life and liberty as well.
rationales.C: Taxes fund government; they are not the property Locke says government exists to preserve.
rationales.D: Colonial trade is far too narrow. Locke's property is the whole bundle of a person's rights and goods.
rationales.general:
1. Read Locke's phrase in full. Government exists to preserve the people's property.
2. Recall Locke's definition. Background: his property is life, liberty, and estate — the broad goods of a person, not just land.
3. Test the narrow options. Land, taxes, and trade goods each cover only a slice of what Locke means.
Remember: when Locke says property, think of the whole bundle — life, liberty, and estate — not one item in it.
